item.title: Venus ate its moon: How Earth's 'twin' could have swallowed a rocky satellite
item.description: Scientists have long speculated why Venus, with a size, mass and structure similar to Earth's, doesn't have a moon. New UC Riverside research shows that our hungry twin likely swallowed it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Durante décadas pensamos que los hombres cazaban y las mujeres cuidaban. La genética cuenta una historia mucho más compleja
item.description: Durante décadas, la arqueología estuvo influida por interpretaciones androcéntricas, puesto que la imagen tradicional que ha llegado hasta nuestros días nos dibujaba un pasado rígido en el que el hombre salía a cazar, mientras la mujer se quedaba cuidando a la prole en el asentamiento. Sin embargo, el estudio del ADN está cambiando la interpretación de la organización social prehistórica. Un nuevo estudio. Ahora la arqueología está revisando estas interpretaciones demasiado centradas en los hombres. Pero la prehistoria no fue generalmente matriarcal, sino que la evidencia demuestra una gran… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: To understand the solar cycle, notice how the sun sleeps
item.description: The sun is such a constant in our lives that it can be difficult to imagine our star ever changing. But the sun can be quite variable. There are times when its magnetic field is turbulent and generates many sunspots and other times when it is quiet and dormant. Since the 1800s, we've known that these active and passive periods follow an 11-year pattern known as the solar cycle. But even after centuries of observation, we still have a difficult time predicting exactly when solar maximum will occur and just how intense it will be. This is important because solar activity can have a significant… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Virtual cells built from 4D AI models and 'digital twins' could speed up drug discovery
item.description: Mitochondria—tiny structures that convert nutrients into energy—are often depicted as discrete kidney bean-shaped objects. But in reality, they form a dynamic, interconnected network throughout the entire cell, rapidly splitting and fusing as they're transported to where energy is needed most. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Magma influx explains short-lived bulge at Tanzania's Ol Doinyo Lengai volcano
item.description: In 2024, D. Sarah Stamps' team detected and tracked a short-lived bulge in the land around a volcano in Tanzania. In a paper published Sep. 18, Stamps identified the cause of the uplift: 1 million cubic meters of magma pouring into an existing magma reservoir about 1.8 miles (2.9 kilometers) underground. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare earth exposure can triple low birthweight risk: Chinese study
item.description: A new study finds that prenatal exposure to rare earth elements can raise the risk of low birthweight, with some substances increasing the danger by more than three times. Researchers tracked 4,891 pregnant women who gave birth at Wuhan Maternal and Child Health Hospital between 2012 and 2014. They measured the concentration of 13 rare earth elements including cerium, ytterbium, and lanthanum in urine samples collected from the mothers. After adjusting for confounding factors such as maternal... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Longitudinal survey finds little evidence that social tech predicts life satisfaction in adults
item.description: Social technologies, digital tools that allow people to communicate and share content with each other online, have become a central way of communicating for many people worldwide. Yet the possible effects of these technologies on the well-being and life satisfaction of regular users are still widely debated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Este delfín ha encontrado una forma bastante repugnante de conseguir comida: hacer vomitar a sus presas
item.description: Los delfines han sido vistos por muchos como seres marinos realmente pacíficos y muy adorables, pero la realidad es que cuentan con diferentes técnicas que no cumplen con esta idealización. Y uno de ellos, la verdad, es que ha sorprendido, sobre todo por lo original que es a la hora de cazar una presa para comérsela. El método de 'Bubbles'. La investigación que ha acaparado un gran protagonismo ha surgido este mismo mes de septiembre a través de la revista Ecology and Evolution . Aquí los investigadores hicieron un seguimiento de la fauna marina y centraron su atención en un macho de delfín… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Satellites show Earth lost more than 12 trillion tons of ice from Greenland, Antarctica in 47 years
item.description: About 12.5 trillion tons (11.3 trillion metric tons) of ice from glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica have melted since 1979, which is enough frozen water to stack ice 5 feet (1.5 meters) deep across the continental United States, according to a major scientific report. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 8 common food additives linked to high blood pressure and heart disease
item.description: Common preservatives hiding in processed foods may carry unexpected heart risks, with heavy consumption linked to substantially higher rates of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease. Researchers identified eight widely used preservatives associated with hypertension, although the observational study cannot prove they were directly responsible. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
item.description: Cats may identify one another through a surprisingly durable chemical “calling card” made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. The compounds appear linked to mysterious fat droplets in the kidneys and may represent a scent-recognition system shared across the cat family. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists may have solved a 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls mystery
item.description: Researchers may have solved a long-running mystery surrounding the Dead Sea Scrolls by proposing that the Qumran sect really did use its distinctive 364-day calendar. Its perfectly ordered 52-week system kept holidays on the same weekdays, but it slowly drifted out of sync with the seasons because it was shorter than the true solar year. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New nanoparticles make hidden chemical differences light up
item.description: Scientists have developed ultra-bright nanoparticles that can detect tiny amounts of chemicals and distinguish between molecules that look almost identical. The technology could one day provide a cheaper way to catch dangerous drug impurities or trace pollutants using simple low-cost lasers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists opened a sealed envelope after 10 years. Gravity still didn’t make sense
item.description: A decade-long NIST experiment has produced a new measurement of the universal gravitational constant that differs unexpectedly from another leading result, deepening a 225-year-old physics puzzle. The discrepancy is tiny, but for one of nature’s most fundamental constants, it is large enough to keep scientists wondering whether hidden experimental errors or something more surprising is involved. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ancient DNA reveals how plague kept returning for 400 years after the Black Death
item.description: Ancient DNA reveals that plague repeatedly returned to Europe for more than 400 years after the Black Death, evolving into new lineages and spreading through trade, migration, and war. Researchers also developed a method to date ancient plague genomes more precisely, linking many of them to specific outbreaks recorded in historical sources. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
item.description: Chemical clues preserved inside fossilized T. rex teeth reveal that the dinosaur maintained a body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit, almost identical to humans. The finding provides direct evidence that the giant predator was warm-blooded, helping explain how it stayed active and survived in chilly environments as far north as Alaska. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Einstein’s “spooky action” just survived one of physics’ most extreme tests
item.description: Physicists have detected strong evidence that heavy, fleeting Z bosons can become quantum entangled during Higgs boson decays at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. The result shows that Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” survives even under some of the most extreme conditions ever created in a laboratory. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Hidden gut defect that may explain why IBD keeps coming back
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a hidden molecular warning sign of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that can linger even when patients feel well and appear to be in remission. By studying around 900 human gut biopsies and patient-derived mini-intestines, the team found that intestinal cells can remain unusually primed to die, creating a “smoldering” defect that may help drive future flare-ups. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: Across Appalachia and the Rust Belt region, including throughout the city of Pittsburgh, former industrial sites are being transformed into new neighborhoods, research centers and technology hubs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How the malaria parasite boosts its transmission potential under stress conditions
item.description: The malaria parasite is able to detect changes in its host's environment and respond by increasing the production of sexual forms capable of being transmitted to mosquitoes. A study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) identifies the molecular mechanism underlying this process. The findings, published in Nature Microbiology, answer what has been one of the major unanswered questions in malaria research for decades. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sacred springs of South Africa—pure waters or polluted? We found tiny bits of plastic in the samples we tested
item.description: Across South Africa, natural springs are more than sources of freshwater. Some are places of healing, spiritual cleansing and rituals, where communities collect water and maintain longstanding cultural connections with the environment. For example, during cleansing rituals, people bathe in or collect spring water as a way of seeking spiritual renewal, healing and protection. These are known as sacred springs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two-color light steers electrons through graphene's transient topological state
item.description: The electronic properties of materials are typically determined by their structure under normal, undisturbed conditions, when they are in a state known as equilibrium. Intense light beams, however, can temporarily reshape a material's electronic band structure (i.e., the range of energy states available to electrons), potentially giving rise to new electronic behaviors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A molecular bridge connects two signaling pathways critical for pollen development
item.description: Cells rely on complex signaling networks in which different molecular pathways communicate with one another. Small GTPases act as molecular switches in these networks, controlling diverse cellular processes such as intracellular transport and cell morphogenesis. Although crosstalk between different families of small GTPases is established in animal cells, whether and how such crosstalk occurs in plants has remained largely unknown. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australia's vast Nullarbor Plain hides deep caves that can teach us about alien worlds
item.description: Stretching more than 200,000 square kilometers (77,000 square miles) across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world's largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black Eye Galaxy Image: Webb and Hubble reveal dusty star-forming band; traces ancient merger
item.description: Located roughly 17 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Coma Berenices, M64 is known for an unusual internal motion: gas in its outer regions rotates in the opposite direction to the gas and stars closer to the centre. NASA says this counter-rotation may be a remnant of a merger involving M64 and a smaller satellite galaxy more than a billion years ago. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Bringing ice sheets to life: Releasing a dynamic ice sheet modeling workflow for Australia's climate model
item.description: Ice sheets are fundamental components of the Earth system. Antarctica and Greenland, the two ice sheets currently on Earth, don't just affect their own regions: What happens on these vast masses of land ice influences weather, climate, society and the environment around the planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global population dataset uses buildings to reveal people's daily movement patterns
item.description: Researchers at the Department of Energy's (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) have released LandScan Mosaic, a next-generation global population distribution dataset that estimates where people are by modeling how buildings are used and occupied throughout the day. Built on the foundation of ORNL's widely used LandScan Global, one of the world's most accurate population distribution datasets, Mosaic's enhancements will improve disaster response, humanitarian assistance, infrastructure planning and national security missions worldwide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is China’s fabled Empress Dowager Huayang buried near an airport? A study says yes
item.description: An airport is an unlikely place to search for national origins but researchers say they have uncovered the tomb of the woman behind the man who unified China – next to a major city runway. The researchers said the tomb was believed to belong to Empress Dowager Huayang, the adoptive grandmother of Qin Shi Huang, who unified the warring states more than 2,200 years ago. “I believe the most likely identity of the tomb owner is Empress Dowager Huayang,” Zhao Hanqing, from the Shaanxi Provincial... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Meet Earth's newest wild cat species, the first named in over a century
item.description: A previously unknown cat species has been identified in plain sight: at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia, where the small, spotted feline had been living for years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A humpback whale was spotted in a California river, 60 miles from its Pacific Ocean home
item.description: Denny Glover was hoping for a big catch when he went fishing with buddies on the Sacramento River, but he wasn't expecting a fully grown humpback whale. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The monsters that weren't: Dinosaur and tusked-beast claims in San rock art unravel
item.description: For decades, an idea has grown in paleontology that, long before scientists began digging up and reconstructing dinosaur bones, the Indigenous San and Basotho in southern Africa noticed them too, incorporating them into songs, myths and immortalizing them on cave walls. But under closer scrutiny, these claims begin to crumble. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rethinking how we assess students could improve their well-being
item.description: When you were in school, what stressed you out the most? For many students, classroom assessments—graded tests, quizzes, group work, presentations, labs and the like—would be near the top of the list. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Florida scrub-jays attempt to breed at unusually young age after large-scale translocation
item.description: For nearly two decades, biologist Lauren Deaner has worked with Florida scrub-jays, contributing to population recovery efforts and translocations. Now, as a doctoral researcher in UCF's integrative biology program, she is using that field experience to investigate how genetics, behavior and population dynamics influence the long-term recovery of imperiled species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New chemical wipes out 95% of termites without harming humans
item.description: A chemical that stops drywood termites from building new exoskeletons killed about 95% of colonies in testing, offering a potentially safer alternative to traditional fumigation. Because termites eventually have no choice but to molt, the treatment turns a normal stage of their life cycle into a fatal weakness. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A giant crater may reveal the origin of Mars’ doomed moon
item.description: A massive crater on Mars’ moon Phobos may hide a dense region of compressed material that could reveal whether the moon is a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact on Mars. Japan’s upcoming MMX sample return mission could provide the measurements and physical evidence needed to solve the mystery. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: This deep-sea enzyme survives heat that destroys most proteins
item.description: A deep-sea microbe uses an exceptionally heat-resistant enzyme to turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia at temperatures that would destroy most proteins. Its unusual structure and a newly observed reaction state may reveal an ancient, shared mechanism behind nitrogen fixation and could eventually inspire cleaner biotechnology and fertilizer production. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Protein map reveals how red blood cells rapidly adjust to low oxygen
item.description: Scientists map the hidden protein network that helps red blood cells adapt to oxygen Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This tiny organism can shrink to one quarter its size in milliseconds
item.description: A single-celled organism can shrink to one-quarter of its length in milliseconds using a remarkable calcium-powered protein “fishnet.” Scientists hope its unusual machinery could inspire artificial muscles capable of moving far faster than today’s designs. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists find that “perfect” systems may be surprisingly fragile
item.description: Complex systems may work better when their parts are not perfectly alike. Northwestern physicists found that carefully balanced variation, or “disorder,” can make networks such as power grids, ecosystems, neurons, and materials more stable. Even random differences sometimes improved stability compared with completely uniform systems. The discovery could help researchers design more resilient technologies and explain why natural systems are so rarely perfectly uniform. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Loss of Y chromosome in men could be an early warning sign of cancer
item.description: A study initiated by Dr. Dan Theodorescu, a physician-scientist at the University of Arizona Cancer Center, revealed that the loss of the Y chromosome in men's body tissue could pave the way for cancer to develop. According to research recently published in JCI Insights, the loss of the chromosome, which is common in men as they age, creates a preneoplastic field effect, a hidden zone of genetic vulnerability in normal tissue that provides fertile ground for cancer to develop. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists simulate cosmic crashes to test whether icy moons gain or lose their ability to sustain life
item.description: Many of the moons orbiting Saturn, Uranus and Neptune likely conceal oceans of liquid water beneath miles of icy shell. Because life as we know it needs water, these buried oceans rank among the most promising places to search for life beyond Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kids involved with child protective services miss much more school than their peers
item.description: Across the country, kids are settling into new school-year routines. Parents buy backpacks, teachers arrange desks and lesson plans, and friends reconnect. But in recent years, empty chairs are becoming a more common sight—especially in classrooms where students are already facing the most adversity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MIT robot builds working laser cavity in 50 maneuvers under 30 minutes, self-corrects after disruption
item.description: Massachusetts Institute of Technology researchers developed a robotic optics laboratory. This system autonomously assembles and aligns laser cavities with precision. The robot can also correct experimental setups after they are disturbed. This technology could accelerate testing for various optical devices and materials. Future applications envision remote interaction with these automated research environments. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Scientists solve a 50-year mystery and discover a new human blood group
item.description: Scientists have identified the genetic cause behind the mysterious AnWj blood group antigen, solving a puzzle that began in 1972 and establishing a new blood group system called MAL. The discovery could make it much easier to find extremely rare AnWj-negative patients and donors and protect them from potentially dangerous transfusion reactions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sea surface temperature biases shift the North Pacific jet stream southward, study finds
item.description: Climate models are numerical models used to project future climate change. They simulate the climate from the present into the future by calculating changes in the atmosphere, ocean and other components of the climate system. However, simulations of the present-day climate do not perfectly reproduce observations and contain various biases. The model characteristics that cause these biases can also affect simulations of the future climate. Understanding the causes and impacts of present-day climate biases is therefore important for improving the reliability of future climate projections. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover first new wild cat in more than 100 years
item.description: Scientists have identified a previously unknown species of wild cat living at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia. The tiny, spotted feline had lived at the sanctuary for years before genetic analysis revealed it as the first new living wild cat species identified in more than a century. Publicado también por: Sky News - World. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: Fourteen tail vertebrae found in Spain replaces North America as the only Diplodocus site
item.description: A significant paleontological breakthrough has occurred in Spain, where researchers have identified the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils beyond North America. Found in Teruel, these tail vertebrae date back around 150 million years. The discovery implies that during the Late Jurassic era, declining sea levels could have permitted dinosaurs to migrate between continents. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Scientists discover the first diplodocus ever found outside North America
item.description: A 150-million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Spain has been identified as the first confirmed Diplodocus ever found outside North America. The giant sauropod measured about 25 meters long and was preserved well enough for researchers to match distinctive features in its tail bones to the famous genus. Its unexpected appearance in Europe suggests dinosaurs were moving between the continents during the Late Jurassic, possibly across temporary land connections. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How rural policing gaps can make escaping domestic violence harder
item.description: Before murdering Molly Ticehurst in April 2024, court documents show Daniel Billings had threatened to exploit the limits of policing in her country town: "I will come in the middle of the night … The police won't stop me. I will get to you quicker than they will." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Billions in rare earth elements may be hiding in America’s coal ash
item.description: Scientists are looking to diatoms, sea sponges, and plants for a cleaner way to recover rare earth elements and other valuable minerals hidden inside coal ash, red mud, and mine tailings. The bio-inspired approach could turn massive industrial waste piles into useful materials while reducing energy use, harsh chemicals, and reliance on new mining. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese scientists find first evidence of ancient nose-chopping punishment for cattle thieves
item.description: Stealing someone’s cattle is a serious crime, and in many places, the thief would end up in jail. However, ancient Chinese justice could result in a truly horrific form of mutilation: the amputation of the nose. This harsh consequence has been well-documented by historians as one of the infamous “five punishments” from the penal system of the Xia dynasty (2070 BC–1600 BC). Until now, no physical evidence of this punishment had been discovered. A team of researchers from China and the US recently... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Peer sexual harassment emerges early, highlighting need for prevention before Grade 4
item.description: Sexual harassment between peers begins as early as Grade 4 and continues throughout lower secondary school. Most of those who sexually harass others have also experienced harassment themselves. These are among the findings of a doctoral thesis in psychology by Aziz-Kaan Dönmez from the University of Gothenburg, who studied peer sexual harassment among Swedish children and adolescents in Grades 4–9. Dönmez will defend his thesis on October 2. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: El tilcayo, un pequeño gato moteado que habita en los bosques nublados de los Yungas, fue reconocido como una especie distinta tras un análisis genético. El hallazgo, publicado en la revista científica Current Biology, es el primero de este tipo desde 1923. Hasta ahora, la presencia del animal solo ha sido confirmada en Bolivia. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Medieval Chinese skeleton may reveal first evidence of a brutal punishment
item.description: Ancient Chinese authorities used many creative ways to punish people, often with methods designed to mark them for life. One brutal example mentioned repeatedly in historical texts is cutting off a person's nose. However, archaeologists in China have never found skeletal evidence to prove that it occurred. But that may have changed following the discovery of a skeleton of a woman who lived in China about 700 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Workplace AI adoption remains slow, informal and uneven, survey finds
item.description: Despite the rapid development of generative AI and the high level of public interest, the use of AI in the day-to-day work of many employees is not yet the norm. This is the finding of the third wave of the Konstanz AI study, for which a total of 1,105 employees were surveyed in May 2026. The proportion of employees who use AI in their work rose only slightly from 35% to 38% compared with the previous year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: To read 2,000-year-old burned scrolls, scientists burn their own
item.description: Douglas Seiler painstakingly sourced papyrus and reed pens from Egypt and traditional lampblack ink from Japan, then paid some high school students to inscribe the papyrus with lines from Star Wars and the Bible and a quote from the '60s sci-fi TV show The Outer Limits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Power breeds suspicion: In cases of wrongdoing, people point to leaders more quickly
item.description: People with power are more quickly singled out as the culprit when something goes wrong but it is unclear who made the mistake. That is shown by a series of studies by researchers at the University of Amsterdam. In one, they analyzed almost 100,000 everyday conflicts on the Reddit page "Am I the Asshole?" According to the researchers, people with power are more readily blamed because others think they can "get away with anything." The findings are published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Amino acids and a bone mineral may help control magnesium implant breakdown, three student papers suggest
item.description: Seeing a bachelor's thesis published in a scientific journal is relatively uncommon. For three theses linked to the same research group to result in scientific publications within just three months is downright rare. Yet that is exactly what has happened in Elsebeth Schröder's research group at the Division of Quantum Device Physics. Fuente: Phys.org.
